evals.prompt: I have the titanic passenger data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. I want to test whether the proportion of survivors differed across the three passenger classes (1st, 2nd, 3rd). Walk me through how to do this. My TA also wants me to apply Bonferroni adjustment.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py (or its Python equivalent) to load the parquet, finds and reads titanic_description.md to learn pclass has 3 levels (1st/2nd/3rd, a proxy for socio-economic status) and survived is Yes/No. Decides on lev='Yes' (the conventional positive framing of survival), alt_hyp='two-sided' (since user said 'differed' without a direction), and adjust='bonferroni' as requested. Notes there will be 3 pairwise comparisons (all combinations of pclass). Before running, mentions the chi-squared cell-count assumption: for each pair, all four expected cell counts should be ≥ 5. Fits with rsm.basics.compare_props({'titanic': df}, var1='pclass', var2='survived', lev='Yes', alt_hyp='two-sided', conf=0.95, adjust='bonferroni'), prints summary(extra=True), and walks the output: per-group rates (1st 63.5% survival, 2nd 44.1%, 3rd 26.2%); each pair's hypothesis (H0: equal proportions; Ha: not equal), diff in percentage points, p-value (all < .001 even after Bonferroni since raw p's were tiny), 95% CI (none contain 0), chi-sq.value (all >> 3.841 critical at 1 df). Translates to plain English: 'Socio-economic class was strongly associated with Titanic survival — 1st-class passengers were 37.3 percentage points more likely to survive than 3rd-class (95% CI 30.5pp-44.1pp, p<.001, Bonferroni-adjusted). All three pairwise comparisons confirm the hierarchy.' Optionally mentions that the chi-squared cell-count check is fine here (smallest expected cell ≈ 100, well above 5).

evals.prompt: Same titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. Now I only want to compare 1st vs 2nd class and 1st vs 3rd class — those are the substantive contrasts my prof cares about. Also include the chi-sq.value and CI bounds in the output.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: refits with comb=['1st:2nd', '1st:3rd'] to focus on the 2 substantive contrasts (rather than all 3 pairs), uses summary(extra=True) to display chisq.value, df, and CI columns. Notes that with only 2 pre-specified pairs, Bonferroni is less critical (and the user didn't ask for it this time, so default to None unless the user prefers — explicitly mention this choice). Walks the output: 1st vs 2nd (diff ≈ 19.4 pp, chisq ≈ 20.58 on 1 df, 95% CI [11.2 pp, 27.7 pp], p < .001) and 1st vs 3rd (diff ≈ 37.3 pp, chisq ≈ 104.70 on 1 df, 95% CI [30.5 pp, 44.1 pp], p < .001). Explains the three-way verdict for each: (a) p < .001 << 0.05 → reject; (b) 0 not in CI → reject; (c) chisq >> critical value 3.841 (from prob_calc('chisq', df=1, pub=0.95)) → reject. Explicitly notes that focusing via comb= is the principled alternative to Bonferroni — if the research question pre-specifies which pairs matter, you don't need to correct for the pairs you don't run. The substantive conclusion: 1st-class passengers were dramatically more likely to survive than passengers in either of the other classes.

evals.prompt: I want to test whether the survival rate differed by some rare manifest cabin assignment. I filtered the titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet to just the rows where 'cabin' starts with 'T' — there are only 3 such passengers, all in 1st class, with 1 survivor. I want to compare survival between this 'cabin-T' group (n=3, survived=1) and the rest of 1st class (n≈279, survived≈178). The p-value came back as roughly 0.4 — does that mean cabin-T didn't matter?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) IMMEDIATELY flags the chi-squared cell-count assumption violation as the central issue, not the p-value; (2) walks through the implicit 2x2 table: |cabin-T: survived=1, died=2; rest-1st: survived≈178, died≈101|, computes pooled p ≈ (1+178)/(3+279) ≈ 0.635, then expected cells: 3*0.635=1.9 (survived in cabin-T), 3*0.365=1.1 (died in cabin-T), 279*0.635=177.2 (survived in rest), 279*0.365=101.8 (died in rest); (3) FLAGS that the smallest expected cell (1.1) is far below the rule-of-thumb threshold of 5 — the chi-squared / z-test approximation is unreliable here regardless of what p-value pyrsm prints; (4) explains why the test is unreliable: with such tiny expected counts, the discrete sampling distribution is not well-approximated by the normal/chi-squared, so the p-value (whether 0.4 or anything else) is misleading; (5) recommends Fisher's exact test as the proper alternative: from scipy.stats import fisher_exact; odds_ratio, p_fisher = fisher_exact([[1, 2], [178, 101]]) — give the user the code; (6) ALSO notes the broader issue: n=3 is just too small for any test to yield strong conclusions about whether cabin-T 'matters' for survival — even if the test were valid, the power to detect any reasonable effect size would be tiny; (7) refuses to interpret the p ≈ 0.4 as 'cabin-T didn't matter' — that's a fail-to-reject masquerading as a positive null finding, which the small n cannot support; (8) recommends either pooling cabin-T with adjacent cabin groups (collapse) or treating this as an exploratory observation rather than a hypothesis test.
